$B_1A_1=0$, $B_iA_i=A_{i-1}B_{i-1}$ $(2\le i<t)$. Then $Z$ is a complete
intersection, smooth outside a closed subset of codimension $\ge2$, reduced,
irreducible and normal, and the invariant ring $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ under
$H=\prod_{i<t}\mathrm{GL}(U_i)$ is the coordinate ring of $X$ via the end map
$\theta=A_{t-1}B_{t-1}$.

An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every commutative Noetherian integrally closed domain satisfies $(S_2)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring and let $M\ne0$ be a finite
$R$-module. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}(M)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Ass}_R(M).$$

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $M$ be a finitely generated left
$R$-module, and let $S \subseteq R$ be multiplicative. Then
$$ \operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}M)=\{S^{-1}\mathfrak p : \mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_R(M),\ \mathfrak p \cap S=\varnothing\}. $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $R$ be Noetherian, let $M$ be finite, let $I$ lie in the Jacobson radical,
and let $x\in I$ be $M$-regular. Then
$$\operatorname{depth}_I(M/xM)=\operatorname{depth}_I(M)-1,$$
with $\infty-1=\infty$.

Assume Dependent Choice. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring and let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Then
the set of zero divisors on $M$ is
$$ \bigcup_{\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_R(M)}\mathfrak p. $$
If the Axiom of Choice also holds and $M$ is finitely generated, this is a finite union.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $I \trianglelefteq R$ be an ideal, and let
$\mathfrak p_1,\dots,\mathfrak p_n$ be prime ideals with $n \ge 1$. If
$$ I\subseteq \mathfrak p_1\cup\cdots\cup \mathfrak p_n, $$
then $I\subseteq \mathfrak p_i$ for some $i$.

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, let $n\ge0$, and let
$E:=V^{\otimes n}$ carry the left place action of $S_n$
([[def-commuting-symmetric-and-linear-actions-on-tensor-power]]). Let $A$ be
the image of the algebra homomorphism $\mathbb C[S_n]\to\operatorname{End}(E)$
extending the place action, and let
$B:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$
be the linear span of the diagonal operators
$g^{\otimes n}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n$.
Then:

1. **(Mutual centralizers.)** $B=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F a=aF\text{ for
   all }a\in A\}$ and $A=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):F b=bF\text{ for all
   }b\in B\}$.
2. **(Uniqueness of the identification.)** $B$ is a unital
   $\mathbb C$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(E)$ and equals the image of
   the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
   $U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$, that is the unital subalgebra generated by the
   operators $\Delta(T)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes
   \mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}$, $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$
   ([[lem-tensor-place-operators-span-the-symmetric-centralizer]]).

All statements include $n=0$, where $E=\mathbb C$.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

derivations.claim: Hartogs lifting. Let $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and let $f\in\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ be regular on $O$, hence regular off a closed subset of $X\setminus O$; since $\partial X$ has codimension $\ge2$ in $X$ by the normality lemma [F1], $f$ is regular in codimension $1$ and therefore extends to $A$ by [F2]. Applying this coordinatewise to maps into a finite-dimensional vector space shows that every regular map $O\to W$ into a finite-dimensional vector space extends uniquely to a regular map $X\to W$.

The equivariant map on $O$. Fix $B\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})^{G_e}$ and define, for $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $F(g\,e\,g^{-1}):=(g^{\otimes d})\,B\,(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. This is well defined: if $g_1e g_1^{-1}=g_2eg_2^{-1}$, then $g_2^{-1}g_1\in G_e$, so $(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{\otimes d}B(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{-\otimes d}=B$ by $G_e$-invariance, which rearranges to $(g_1^{\otimes d})B(g_1^{-1})^{\otimes d}=(g_2^{\otimes d})B(g_2^{-1})^{\otimes d}$. The map $F$ is $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant by construction: $F(hXh^{-1})=(h^{\otimes d})F(X)(h^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ for $X\in O$.

Regularity of $F$ on $O$. The ranks of $X^0,X^1,\dots,X^{l-1}$ are constant on $O$. Cover $O$ by open charts where fixed minors used to select bases of the kernels and images, their quotient complements and Jordan top vectors are nonzero. Gaussian elimination on such a chart gives a Jordan basis for $X$ with entries regular in $X$. Let $g(X)$ carry a fixed Jordan basis for $e$ to this chosen Jordan basis for $X$, with the same ordered string lengths. Then $g(X)e g(X)^{-1}=X$. Restricting to the open chart where the Jordan-basis determinant is nonzero makes both $g(X)$ and $g(X)^{-1}$ regular, since their entries have only the fixed nonvanishing minors and determinant as denominators. Thus $X\mapsto(g(X)^{\otimes d})B(g(X)^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ is the map of step 1.2 and is regular on each chart. These charts cover $O$; on overlaps $g_2(X)^{-1}g_1(X)\in G_e$, so the expressions agree by $G_e$-invariance of $B$. Hence $F$ is regular on $O$.

Extension to $X$. By steps 1.2 and 2.1 the map $F\colon O\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ is a regular equivariant map on the dense orbit; by step 1.1 it extends uniquely to a regular map $F\colon X\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. Since $\mathbb C[X]=\mathbb C[\operatorname{End}(V)]/I(X)$ and $X$ is an affine closed subset of the affine space $\operatorname{End}(V)$, the coordinate functions of $F$ are restrictions of polynomial functions on $\operatorname{End}(V)$; fixing representatives gives a polynomial map $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ extending $F$.

Equivariance of $\Phi$. For fixed $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, both sides of $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ are polynomial maps in $X$; they agree on the dense orbit $O$ by step 1.2 and hence on all of $X$. Consequently the class of $\Phi$ in the finite-dimensional space of polynomial maps $\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ of degree at most $K$ (for $K$ at least the degree of $\Phi$), modulo the $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-stable subspace of maps vanishing on $X$, is invariant for the conjugation action. By the invariant-lifting property of complete reducibility [F3], this class has an invariant representative $\Phi'$ of degree at most $K$; then $\Phi'$ is a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map on $\operatorname{End}(V)$ agreeing with $F$ on $X$, and $\Phi'(e)=F(e)=B$ since $e\in O$, which is assertion (1).

Polarization. Write $\Phi=\sum_k\Phi_k$ for its homogeneous components of degree $k$; each $\Phi_k$ is equivariant. Fix $k$ and assume for the structure argument that $\Phi$ is homogeneous of degree $k$. Polarize the $k$ matrix variables $X_1,\dots,X_k$ of $\Phi$ and pair the output in $\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ with $d$ independent matrices $Y_1,\dots,Y_d$ using the nondegenerate trace pairing on each tensor factor; this produces a multilinear $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-invariant $P(X_1,\dots,X_k;Y_1,\dots,Y_d)\in\mathbb C$ in $(k+d)$ matrix arguments.

Tensor invariants are permutation contractions. By the Schur-Weyl description [F3], every multilinear invariant of the matrix arguments is a linear combination of contractions: each argument contributes one upper and one lower index, an invariant pairs each upper index with a lower index of another argument, and the invariant is a product over the cycles of the resulting permutation of traces of the corresponding cyclically ordered product of matrices.

Covariant normal form. Depolarize in the $k$ identical variables $X_i=X$ and read each contraction cycle. A cycle that uses only $X$-arguments contributes a scalar invariant polynomial in $X$; a cycle that uses some $Y$-arguments alternates blocks of $X$'s and single $Y$'s, so its trace is precisely the trace pairing of $Y_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Y_d$ with a place permutation of $X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d}$. By nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, the operator identity $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ follows, with $h_i\ge0$, $\sigma_h$ a place permutation and $c_h$ a scalar invariant polynomial (a polynomial in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^m)$); summing over the homogeneous components gives assertion (2).

Evaluation at $e$. Since $e^l=0$ for the largest Jordan block length $l$ of $e$, evaluating the normal form at $X=e$ kills every term with some $h_i\ge l$; the surviving terms are place permutations applied to a tensor product of nonnegative powers $e^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{h_d}$ multiplied by the scalar invariants $c_h(e)$, which are ordinary numbers depending only on the Jordan type of $e$ (that is, on the list of eigenvalues $\operatorname{tr}(e^m)$, all zero for nilpotent $e$, so $c_h(e)=c_h(0)$). This gives the concrete description of the $G_e$-fixed endomorphisms used by the double centralizer theorem.

Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the Casimir element of
[[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
and its operator on every $\mathfrak g$-module is the image under the
representation, commuting with the $\mathfrak g$-action
([[lem-the-casimir-operator-is-basis-independent-and-intertwining]],
[[lem-the-casimir-element-is-independent-of-dual-bases]]).

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $0\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$ (so $z_M$ acts as the representation of the
central element $z$ of $\mathfrak g$).

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

determined by

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}((m\otimes n)\otimes p)=m\otimes(n\otimes p).$$

It respects any compatible outer module actions and is natural in $M,N,P$.

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Work over the field $\mathbb C$ and fix an integer $d\ge 0$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-commutative-ring]]). Let
$\mathcal F_d$ be the free associative unital $\mathbb C$-algebra on the
$d+(d-1)$ symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ (for $d=0$ there is only
the unit; for $d=1$ only $x_1$), with its word basis and universal property
([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]), and let
$I_d\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}\mathcal F_d$ be the two-sided ideal
([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]])
generated by the following elements:

- $x_ix_j-x_jx_i$ for all $1\le i,j\le d$;
- $s_i^2-1$, $s_is_{i+1}s_i-s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$, and $s_is_j-s_js_i$ for
  $|i-j|>1$, for $1\le i,j\le d-1$;
- $s_ix_j-x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$, $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i-1$, and
  $x_{i+1}s_i-s_ix_i-1$, for $1\le i\le d-1$ and $1\le j\le d$.

The **degenerate affine Hecke algebra** is the quotient $\mathbb C$-algebra
$$H_d:=\mathcal F_d/I_d$$
with unit element written $1$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]). We keep the symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ for their images, and for $w\in S_d$ we write
$w$ for the image in $H_d$ of any word in the $s_i$ representing $w$; this is
independent of the chosen word once the basis theorem below is proved. For
$a\in\mathbb C$, the notation $H_d/(x_1-a)$ means the quotient by the two-sided
ideal generated by $x_1-a$.

The verification below establishes exactly the structure of $H_d$ used
throughout this page: the ordered monomials
$$x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w,\qquad r_1,\dots,r_d\ge0,\ w\in S_d,$$
form a $\mathbb C$-basis, so that
$H_d\cong\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]$ as a vector
space with polynomial and group-algebra subalgebras
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]], [[def-group-ring]]);
$H_0=\mathbb C$ and $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$; for every $a$ there is a unique
algebra isomorphism
$$H_d/(x_1-a)\cong\mathbb C[S_d],\qquad x_j\longmapsto a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j);$$
and total polynomial degree is an algebra filtration whose associated graded is
the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which
$s_i$ acts by swapping $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$. The cross relation is
inhomogeneous, so it does not turn $H_d$ into a graded algebra with
$\deg x_i=1$ and $\deg s_i=0$.

The Casimir element $\Omega_B$ is independent of the chosen dual bases and
belongs to the center of $U(\mathfrak g)$. Consequently its action on every
$\mathfrak g$-module is a $\mathfrak g$-intertwiner.

For a vector space $V$ over $k$, write

$$\mathfrak{gl}(V)=\operatorname{End}_k(V)$$

with commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Expansion of triple composites shows
that this is a Lie algebra in every characteristic.

A **representation** of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ on $V$ is a Lie-algebra
homomorphism

$$\rho:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak{gl}(V).$$

Writing $xv$ for $\rho(x)(v)$, this is equivalently a $k$-bilinear action
$\mathfrak g\times V\to V$ satisfying

$$[x,y]v=x(yv)-y(xv)$$

for all $x,y\in\mathfrak g$ and $v\in V$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis is
imposed on either $\mathfrak g$ or $V$. The zero vector space and the zero
action are allowed.

derivations.claim: The infinitesimal braid identities. For distinct labels $a,b,c$ one has $[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{ac}+\Omega_{bc}]=0$: expanding $\Omega=\sum E_{uv}\otimes E_{vu}$ and using [F3], the double commutator sum splits into terms $[E_{uv},E_{xy}]\otimes E_{vu}\otimes E_{yx}$ and $E_{uv}\otimes[E_{vu},E_{xy}]\otimes E_{yx}$, and the two resulting sums cancel term by term after relabelling; equivalently, this is the identity $[\Omega_{12},\Omega_{13}+\Omega_{23}]=0$ in $U(\mathfrak g)^{\otimes3}$, which is the derivative of the invariance of $\Omega$ under the diagonal adjoint action. Consequently $[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{ac}]=-[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{bc}]=[\Omega_{ac},\Omega_{bc}]$. In particular, for three natural factors this is the identity $[P_{ab},P_{ac}]+[P_{ab},P_{bc}]=0$ for the flips.

The Coxeter relations for $s_i$. $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ is an involution; $s_is_j=s_js_i$ for $|i-j|>1$ because the pairs of interchanged labels are disjoint; and $s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$ because both sides are the permutation operator inducing the same permutation of the three labelled factors.

Cross relations. Conjugation by $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ interchanges the labels $i$ and $i+1$ in any operator supported on those factors, so $s_i\Omega_{0,i+1}=\Omega_{0i}s_i$ and $s_iP_{k,i+1}=P_{ki}s_i$ for $k<i$. Therefore $s_ix_{i+1}=s_i\Omega_{0,i+1}+\sum_{k<i}s_iP_{k,i+1}+s_iP_{i,i+1}=\Omega_{0i}s_i+\sum_{k<i}P_{ki}s_i+1=x_is_i+1$, and symmetrically $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$. For $j<i$, all labels in $x_j$ are disjoint from $\{i,i+1\}$, so $s_i$ commutes with every summand. For $j>i+1$, $\Omega_{0j}$ and the terms $P_{kj}$ with $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ commute with $s_i$, while conjugation by $s_i$ interchanges $P_{ij}$ and $P_{i+1,j}$. Their sum is invariant, so again $s_ix_j=x_js_i$; the two overlapping summands need not commute individually.

Polynomial commutation. Fix $i<j$. Since $x_i=\Omega_{0i}+\sum_{k<i}P_{ki}$ and $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{l<j}P_{lj}$, the commutator is $[\Omega_{0i},\Omega_{0j}]+\sum_{l<j}[\Omega_{0i},P_{lj}]+\sum_{k<i}[P_{ki},\Omega_{0j}]+\sum_{k<i}\sum_{l<j}[P_{ki},P_{lj}]$. The second sum reduces to the single term $[\Omega_{0i},P_{ij}]$ (all other $P_{lj}$ are disjoint from the labels $0,i$), and the third sum vanishes (all pairs $\{k,i\}$, $\{0,j\}$ are disjoint since $k<i<j$). In the fourth sum only the terms with $k=l$ or $l=i$ can fail to vanish, so it equals $\sum_{k<i}([P_{ki},P_{kj}]+[P_{ki},P_{ij}])$. Hence $[x_i,x_j]=([\Omega_{0i},\Omega_{0j}]+[\Omega_{0i},P_{ij}])+\sum_{k<i}([P_{ki},P_{kj}]+[P_{ki},P_{ij}])$. The first bracket vanishes by step 1.1 with $a=0$, $b=i$, $c=j$ together with $\Omega_{ij}=P_{ij}$; each summand of the second bracket vanishes by step 1.1 for the three distinct labels $k,i,j$. Therefore $[x_i,x_j]=0$.

Naturality, commutation with $\mathfrak g$, and the right action. The place permutations are natural in $M$ and commute with $\mathfrak g$; the Casimir operators are intertwiners by [F5]; hence every $x_j$ and $s_i$ is natural and $\mathfrak g$-linear. The relations established in steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the defining relations of $H_d$ [F4], so the assignment $x_j\mapsto x_j$, $s_i\mapsto s_i$ defines a left $H_d$-action. The generator-fixing anti-automorphism $\omega$ of $H_d$ (which preserves each defining relation because the reversed cross relation $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$ is also a defining relation) converts it into a right action by $e\cdot u:=\rho(\omega(u))e$; the anti-automorphism property gives $(e\cdot u)\cdot v=\rho(\omega(v))\rho(\omega(u))e=\rho(\omega(uv))e=e\cdot(uv)$. This proves both assertions.

An endomorphism $N:V\to V$ is **nilpotent** if $N^k=0$ for some positive integer $k$. Its **nilpotency index** is the least positive integer $r$ such that $N^r=0$; this least exponent exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]).

The unique endomorphism of the zero space is nilpotent. With the same least-positive-exponent convention, its nilpotency index is $1$ because its identity and zero endomorphisms coincide.

Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the Casimir element of
[[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
and its operator on every $\mathfrak g$-module is the image under the
representation, commuting with the $\mathfrak g$-action
([[lem-the-casimir-operator-is-basis-independent-and-intertwining]],
[[lem-the-casimir-element-is-independent-of-dual-bases]]).

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $0\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$ (so $z_M$ acts as the representation of the
central element $z$ of $\mathfrak g$).

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ ([[def-nilpotent-endomorphism]]),
let $X=\overline{\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e}$ be the closure in
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ of its conjugacy orbit
([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]), and let
$\partial X=X\setminus\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e$. Then $\mathbb C[X]$ is a reduced
irreducible normal domain and $\operatorname{codim}_X\partial X\ge2$. This
holds for every Jordan type, not only the regular nilpotent cone.

The proof uses the *chain schemes*: if the Jordan partition of $e$ has column
lengths $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_t>0$, put $n_i=q_t+\cdots+q_{t-i+1}$ and
$U_i=\mathbb C^{n_i}$ for $0\le i\le t$. Let $M=\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}(U_i,U_{i+1})\times\operatorname{Hom}(U_{i+1},U_i)\bigr)$
with coordinates $(A_i,B_i)$ and let $Z\subseteq M$ be the closed subscheme
$B_1A_1=0$, $B_iA_i=A_{i-1}B_{i-1}$ $(2\le i<t)$. Then $Z$ is a complete
intersection, smooth outside a closed subset of codimension $\ge2$, reduced,
irreducible and normal, and the invariant ring $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ under
$H=\prod_{i<t}\mathrm{GL}(U_i)$ is the coordinate ring of $X$ via the end map
$\theta=A_{t-1}B_{t-1}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, let
$G_e=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}(V):geg^{-1}=e\}$ be its centralizer, and let $d\ge0$.

1. Every $G_e$-fixed endomorphism $B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V^{\otimes d})$
   is the value at $e$ of a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map
   $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$
   (polynomial in the matrix entries of the input, with
   $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$).
2. Every such equivariant polynomial map is a finite sum
   $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ with
   $h_i\ge0$, where $\sigma_h$ is a place permutation of the $d$ tensor
   factors and $c_h$ is an invariant scalar polynomial in $X$ (a polynomial
   in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^k)$).

The extension in (1) is proved by Hartogs lifting on the normal codimension-$\ge2$
orbit closure; the structure in (2) is proved by polarization and the
Schur-Weyl description of tensor invariants, not by importing a
first-fundamental-theorem for the full matrix algebra.

Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the Casimir element of
[[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]] is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
and its operator on every $\mathfrak g$-module is the image under the
representation, commuting with the $\mathfrak g$-action
([[lem-the-casimir-operator-is-basis-independent-and-intertwining]],
[[lem-the-casimir-element-is-independent-of-dual-bases]]).

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $0\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$ (so $z_M$ acts as the representation of the
central element $z$ of $\mathfrak g$).

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.

Let $N\ge1$, let $M$ be a $\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$-module, let
$V=\mathbb C^N$ be the natural module, and on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ use the
operators $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ of
[[def-arakawa-suzuki-casimir-operators-on-tensor-functors]]. Then:

1. The operators $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ commute with the
   $\mathfrak g$-action and are natural in $M$, and satisfy all the defining
   relations of the degenerate affine Hecke algebra
   [[def-degenerate-affine-hecke-algebra]]: the Coxeter relations for the
   $s_i$; $s_ix_j=x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ and
   $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$; and the polynomial commutation $[x_i,x_j]=0$.
2. Consequently they define, via the generator-fixing anti-involution of the
   Hecke algebra, a natural right $H_d$-action on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$
   commuting with the left $\mathfrak g$-action.

The commutation of the $x_i$ is an independent check: it does not follow from
the braid relations of the $s_i$ alone.

derivations.claim: The first centralizer. An operator $T\in\operatorname{End}(E)$ commutes with the action of $B$ if and only if it commutes with the individual $e$-operators and with the place permutations: the first condition says $T\in A^{\otimes d}$ by [F2], and then the second says $T\in(A^{\otimes d})^{S_d}$, which is spanned by the elements $a^{\otimes d}$, $a\in A$. The image of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$ under the diagonal representation is contained in $\operatorname{End}_B(E)$: the diagonal action of $A$ commutes with the individual $e$'s and with places. Conversely, for $a\in A$ the element $a^{\otimes d}$ is the value at $1$ of the diagonal action of $\sum_ka_k^{\otimes d}$; Newton's identities express the product $a_1\cdots a_d$ of the commuting operators $a_i=1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes a\otimes1^{\otimes(d-i)}$ as a polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ in the power sums $p_k=\sum_ia_i^k$, $1\le k\le d$, and each $p_k$ is the image under $\varphi$ of $a^k\in U(\mathfrak g^e)$. Hence $a^{\otimes d}\in\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))$ and $\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))=\operatorname{End}_B(E)$.

The second centralizer. An operator $T$ commutes with the diagonal $A$-action if and only if it is $G_e$-fixed, because $G_e=A^\times$ generates $A$ linearly in the diagonal representation: differentiating $t\mapsto(1+ta)^{\otimes d}$ at $t=0$ recovers the diagonal action of $a$, and Newton-type generation is not needed for this direction. By [F3] every $G_e$-fixed operator is $\Phi(e)$ for an equivariant polynomial covariant $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$; evaluating at $X=e$ replaces each $X^{h_i}$ by $e^{h_i}$, which is a polynomial in the individual $e$-operators of degree less than $l$, so $\Phi(e)\in\psi(B)$ (the truncated algebra $B$ contains exactly the polynomials $e^0,\dots,e^{l-1}$ in each factor and the places). Conversely every element of $\psi(B)$ commutes with the diagonal $A$-action: for $a\in A$ put $\Delta_d(a)=\sum_{k=1}^d a^{(k)}$; each individual $e^{(j)}$ satisfies $[\Delta_d(a),e^{(j)}]=[a,e]^{(j)}=0$, and each place permutation $P_\sigma$ satisfies $P_\sigma\Delta_d(a)P_\sigma^{-1}=\Delta_d(a)$. These operators generate $\psi(B)$, so their products and linear combinations also commute with every $\Delta_d(a)$. Therefore $\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g^e}(E)^{\mathrm{op}}=\psi(B)$.

Stable injectivity. Suppose $e$ has at least $d$ Jordan strings of the maximum length $l$, with top vectors $w_1,\dots,w_d$ on distinct strings. The vectors $w_1^{r_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes w_d^{r_d}$ with $0\le r_i<l$ (where $w^r=e^rw$ is the $r$-th vector of the string) are $l^d$ distinct members of the Jordan tensor basis of $E$; applying the $d!$ place permutations gives $l^d d!$ distinct basis vectors, since the string label of each tensor factor is recovered from the vector and the place permutation is recovered from the ordering of the labels. These vectors span a right $B$-submodule isomorphic to the regular module $B$ (the basis vectors $e^{r_1}w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{r_d}w_d\sigma$, $\sigma\in S_d$, multiply exactly as the standard basis of the truncated polynomial/permutation algebra), so the right action $\psi$ is injective. For $d=0$, $E=\mathbb C$, $B=\mathbb C$ and both identities and injectivity reduce to scalar identities.

citations.quote:
Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition
of $N$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l\ge0$, so that $l=p_n$ is the number
of columns, and let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with matrix units
$e_{i,j}$ in the standard basis
$v_1,\dots,v_N$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]). Number the
boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left,
and for a box $i$ write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for its row and
column, $L(i)$ for the box immediately to its left (or $\emptyset$ if absent),
and $R(i)$ for the box immediately to its right (or $\emptyset$ if absent).
Define the nilpotent endomorphism
$$e=\sum_{i:\ L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g,\qquad ev_i=v_{L(i)},$$
and declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ for all $i,j$, so
that $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$ with
$\mathfrak g_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_{i,j}:\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)=r\}$.
Put
$$\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r,\qquad \mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0,\qquad \mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r,$$
and for rows $1\le i,j\le n$ define the shift $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ if $i\le j$
and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$
Finally let $\chi\colon\mathfrak m\to\mathbb C$ be $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$,
where the trace is the trace of the $N\times N$ matrix.

The verification below records the properties of this data that are used
throughout this page. $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$; $\mathfrak p$
is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor
$\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and
nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, while $\mathfrak m$ is the
nilradical of the opposite parabolic; the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ with
$s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ form a basis of the centralizer
$\mathfrak g^e=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,e]=0\}$; the box set
$J=\{(a,b)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$
is in bijection with $K=\{(i,j,r):1\le i,j\le n,\ s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}$ via
$(a,b)\mapsto(\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a))$, and
$$\xi_{a,b}:=\sum_{t=0}^{\mathrm{col}(a)-1}e_{L^t(a),L^t(b)}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)};$$
and $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character, $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$. This
grading is the type-A pyramid good grading of the source, not the Dynkin
grading attached to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

For a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ over $k$ and a $\mathfrak g$-module $M$,
the degree-$n$ **Chevalley–Eilenberg cochains** are

$$C^n(\mathfrak g,M)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\Lambda^n\mathfrak g,M)\quad(n\geq0).$$

Set $C^n(\mathfrak g,M)=0$ for $n<0$. Since
$\Lambda^0\mathfrak g=k$, evaluation at $1$ identifies
$C^0(\mathfrak g,M)$ with $M$. Cochains may equivalently be viewed as
alternating $n$-linear maps $\mathfrak g^n\to M$. No finite-dimensionality
or characteristic hypothesis is needed. If $n>\dim\mathfrak g$ in the
finite-dimensional case, the exterior power and hence the cochain space are
zero.

For $f\in C^n(\mathfrak g,M)$ define $df\in C^{n+1}(\mathfrak g,M)$ by

$$\begin{aligned}(df)(x_0,\ldots,x_n)={}&\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^i x_i f(x_0,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,x_n)\\&+\sum_{0\leq i<j\leq n}(-1)^{i+j}f([x_i,x_j],x_0,\ldots,\widehat{x_i},\ldots,\widehat{x_j},\ldots,x_n).\end{aligned}$$

This fixes a zero-based sign convention. A hat means omission, and in the
second sum the bracket is inserted as the first argument. Empty sums are
zero. Thus for $m\in C^0=M$, $(dm)(x)=xm$. Alternation of the formula makes
it factor through $\Lambda^{n+1}\mathfrak g$; the next theorem proves that
successive differentials compose to zero.

The **Lie algebra cohomology** of $\mathfrak g$ with coefficients in the
$\mathfrak g$-module $M$ is the cohomology of its Chevalley–Eilenberg
cochain complex:

$$H^n(\mathfrak g,M)=\frac{\ker(d:C^n\to C^{n+1})}{\operatorname{im}(d:C^{n-1}\to C^n)}.$$

The containment of the denominator in the numerator is supplied by
[[thm-the-chevalley-eilenberg-differential-squares-to-zero]]. For $n<0$ all
cochain groups, and hence all cohomology groups, are zero by convention. This
definition is valid without finite-dimensionality or a characteristic
restriction.
$$H^0(\mathfrak g,M)=M^{\mathfrak g}=\{m\in M:xm=0\text{ for every }x\in\mathfrak g\}.$$

For finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$ and a short exact sequence
$0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ of $\mathfrak g$-modules, the induced CE
complexes form a degreewise short exact sequence and yield the natural long
exact sequence

$$\cdots\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M')\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M)\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M'')\to H^{n+1}(\mathfrak g,M')\to\cdots.$$

Keep the type-A pyramid data
$(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$ of
[[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]], with
$\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$, transpose
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, and $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$ on $\mathfrak m$.
Let $\eta\colon U(\mathfrak p)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ be the algebra automorphism
with
$$\eta(e_{i,j})=e_{i,j}+\delta_{i,j}\bigl(n-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)}-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)+1}-\cdots-q_l\bigr)$$
for all matrix units $e_{i,j}\in\mathfrak p$. Let $I_\chi$ be the kernel of the
algebra homomorphism $\chi\colon U(\mathfrak m)\to\mathbb C$ extending the Lie
character $\chi$, that is, the two-sided ideal generated by $x-\chi(x)$,
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]),
and let $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ be the left ideal it generates in
$U(\mathfrak g)$.

The **type-A finite W-algebra** is
$$W(\lambda)=\{u\in U(\mathfrak p):[x,\eta(u)]\in U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}.$$
It is a subalgebra of $U(\mathfrak p)$, and
$Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ is a
$(U(\mathfrak g),W(\lambda))$-bimodule with right action
$u\cdot\bar v=\overline{v\,\eta(u)}$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]).

The **Whittaker category** $\mathcal C(\lambda)$ is the category of
$\mathfrak g$-modules on which $x-\chi(x)$ acts locally nilpotently for every
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). For
$M\in\mathcal C(\lambda)$ the **Whittaker vectors**
$$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=\{v\in M:xv=\chi(x)v\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}$$
form a $W(\lambda)$-module with $u\cdot v=\eta(u)v$, and
$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$.

The verification below establishes the algebra and module structures just
stated. The associated graded of the loop filtration on $U(\mathfrak p)$ makes
$W(\lambda)$ a filtered deformation of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$; that statement is
proved later on this page
([[thm-the-loop-filtration-on-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-has-associated-graded-u-of-g-e]]),
and the filtration used is the loop (good) filtration, not the Kazhdan
filtration.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a Lie algebra over $k$. In $T(\mathfrak g)$, regard
$[x,y]\in\mathfrak g$ as an element of tensor degree one, and let $I$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by

$$x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\qquad(x,y\in\mathfrak g).$$

The **universal enveloping algebra** is

$$U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/I.$$

Write

$$\iota_{\mathfrak g}:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow U(\mathfrak g)$$

for the composite of the degree-one inclusion with the quotient map. This
definition makes $U(\mathfrak g)$ a unital associative algebra and $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ a
linear map. It does not assert that $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ is injective; that conclusion will
come from PBW.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $I$ be a set.
The set $R[x_i:i\in I]$ consists of the functions

$$c:\mathcal M(I)\longrightarrow R$$

with finite support, where $\mathcal M(I)$ is the monoid of
[[def-monomials-on-an-index-set]]. We write such a function as the formal sum
$\sum_a c_a x^a$. Addition is pointwise. Multiplication is the convolution

$$(cd)_u:=\sum_{a+b=u}c_a d_b,$$

where only pairs in $\operatorname{supp}(c)\times\operatorname{supp}(d)$
contribute and the sum is the finite sum of
[[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]. The constant $r\in R$ is the
coefficient family supported at the zero monomial with value $r$, and the
indeterminate $x_i$ is supported at the exponent family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere.

The convolution is well defined and these operations make the displayed set a
commutative ring by [[thm-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-is-a-commutative-ring]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: **Positive-weight transverse product.** Choose the usual rowwise $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ triple. On $\operatorname{Hom}(R_b,R_a)$ the strings have highest $h$-weight $p_a+p_b-2k$, $1\le k\le\min(p_a,p_b)$. Since the pyramid grading element differs from $h$ by row scalars, their highest and lowest grading weights are $2(p_b-k)\ge0$ and $-2(p_a-k)\le0$. Thus the negative-degree part is injected by $\operatorname{ad}e$ and gives the direct-sum complement of [F1]. The differential of $\alpha(u,z)=uzu^{-1}$ at $(1,e)$ is $(x,y)\mapsto[x,e]+y$, an isomorphism. Use weight $-H$ on $\mathfrak m$ and weight $2-H$ on the translated slice and target coordinates; these are positive. In homogeneous coordinates of increasing weight, each component of $\alpha$ is an invertible linear block in the variables of that weight plus a polynomial in lower-weight variables. Successive substitution constructs its polynomial inverse. In particular derivative invertibility alone is not being used as a global inverse theorem.

**Detection.** The shifted operators $x-\chi(x)$ form a representation of the nilpotent Lie algebra $\mathfrak m$, because $\chi$ kills brackets. A nonzero central element has a nonzero kernel on any nonzero locally nilpotent module: apply its largest nonvanishing power to a nonzero vector. That kernel is stable, and the quotient Lie algebra acts on it with the same local nilpotence. Induction on $\dim\mathfrak m$ therefore gives a common nonzero invariant. The case $\mathfrak m=0$ is immediate.

**The actual graded complex.** PBW and [F3] give $\operatorname{gr}Q_\chi=\mathbb C[e+\mathfrak m^\perp]$, with no additional symbol factor. Step 1.1 identifies this with $\mathbb C[M_{\mathrm{unip}}]\otimes\mathbb C[S]$. Infinitesimal conjugation acts by invariant vector fields on the first factor and trivially on the slice factor. Giving the exterior dual of a grading-degree $-2r$ vector weight $2r$ makes the twisted Chevalley–Eilenberg differential filtration preserving. Its graded complex is the polynomial de Rham complex of $M_{\mathrm{unip}}$, tensored with $\mathbb C[S]$: invariant vector fields trivialize the tangent bundle and the bracket terms are precisely the de Rham differential. Polynomial exponential coordinates identify this unipotent group with affine space. On a polynomial form of positive total degree $t$, $t^{-1}\iota_{\mathrm{Euler}}$ is a contracting homotopy; constants are the only surviving degree-zero classes.

**Filtered lifting and right freeness.** A positive-degree cocycle in the actual complex has a graded leading term which is a boundary by step 2.1. Lift that boundary and subtract it, strictly lowering the integer filtration degree; boundedness below terminates this process. The same procedure lifts every graded invariant, using vanishing of graded degree-one cohomology to remove its differential. Hence $H^{>0}(\mathfrak m,Q_\chi)=0$ and $\operatorname{gr}W=\mathbb C[S]$, since $H^0(\mathfrak m,Q_\chi)=W$ by the defining invariant realization. Using the fixed PBW vector-space identification $U(\mathfrak p)\to Q_\chi$, take homogeneous coordinate representatives in $U(\mathfrak p)$ and form their ordered products there before projecting to $Q_\chi$. This never multiplies abstract classes in a left-ideal quotient. Their projected ordered monomials, acted on by the right $W$ bimodule action, span $Q_\chi$ by finite descending leading-term subtraction. A finite relation among them would give a relation between distinct monomials over $\operatorname{gr}W$; independence of polynomial monomials rules this out. Thus $Q_\chi$ is right $W$-free. All statements include the independent scalar coordinate of $\mathfrak{gl}_N$.

**Transfer to every module without graded-flatness assumptions.** The finite augmented cochain complex $0\to W\to C^0\to\cdots\to C^{\dim\mathfrak m}\to0$, where $C^j=Q_\chi\otimes\bigwedge^j\mathfrak m^*$, is exact by step 3.1 and is a complex of right $W$-modules. Its differentials are right $W$-linear because the right action commutes with the twisted left $\mathfrak m$ action. Each term is right $W$-free. Starting at the last term, split each surjection onto the already-projective boundary module; descending induction makes every boundary projective and splits every short exact sequence, including $W\hookrightarrow C^0$. These splittings supply a right $W$-linear contraction of the augmented complex. Tensor the contraction with an arbitrary left $W$-module $X$. This remains a contraction, and the resulting complex is exactly the twisted Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of $Q_\chi\otimes_W X$. Consequently its positive cohomology vanishes and its degree-zero cohomology is $X$ via $x\mapsto1_\chi\otimes x$. No filtration or flatness of $X$ is assumed. The splittings use exactly [F4].

The preceding steps prove the three assertions with the doubled even grading. In particular there is no degree $-1$ symplectic or Clifford contribution. If $e=0$, then $\mathfrak m=0$ and the product, augmentation and all cohomology identities reduce to their degree-zero identities.

Keep the pyramid data $(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$
of [[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]] and
the finite W-algebra $W(\lambda)$, the bimodule $Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$
and the Whittaker category of
[[def-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-and-whittaker-category]]. Double the pyramid
grading by declaring the degree of $e_{i,j}$ to be
$2(\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i))$; then $e$ has degree $2$ and the
degree $-1$ part of $\mathfrak g$ is zero. Let
$\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r>0,\ r\ \mathrm{even}}\mathfrak g_{-r}$ in the doubled
grading (the strictly negative even part), carrying the character $\chi$. Then:

1. There is a homogeneous transverse complement
   $S=e+\ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ for a suitable $f\in\mathfrak g$, and the
   conjugation map $M_{\mathrm{unip}}\times S\to e+\mathfrak m^\perp$,
   $(u,s)\mapsto usu^{-1}$, is a polynomial isomorphism; the Kazhdan
   associated graded of $Q_\chi$ is $\mathbb C[M_{\mathrm{unip}}]\otimes\mathbb C[S]$
   and $\operatorname{gr}W(\lambda)=\mathbb C[S]$.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], for every $W(\lambda)$-module $X$, the twisted $\mathfrak m$-cohomology of
   $Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}X$ vanishes in positive degree and its degree-zero
   part is $X$.
3. Every nonzero module on which all $x-\chi(x)$, $x\in\mathfrak m$, act
   locally nilpotently has a nonzero simultaneous invariant vector; in
   particular $\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$ for $M$ in the Whittaker
   category.

These assertions use the doubled good grading; no nondegenerate alternating
form on the original degree $-1$ space is asserted.

Keep the type-A pyramid data
$(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$ of
[[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]], with
$\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$, transpose
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, and $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$ on $\mathfrak m$.
Let $\eta\colon U(\mathfrak p)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ be the algebra automorphism
with
$$\eta(e_{i,j})=e_{i,j}+\delta_{i,j}\bigl(n-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)}-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)+1}-\cdots-q_l\bigr)$$
for all matrix units $e_{i,j}\in\mathfrak p$. Let $I_\chi$ be the kernel of the
algebra homomorphism $\chi\colon U(\mathfrak m)\to\mathbb C$ extending the Lie
character $\chi$, that is, the two-sided ideal generated by $x-\chi(x)$,
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]),
and let $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ be the left ideal it generates in
$U(\mathfrak g)$.

The **type-A finite W-algebra** is
$$W(\lambda)=\{u\in U(\mathfrak p):[x,\eta(u)]\in U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}.$$
It is a subalgebra of $U(\mathfrak p)$, and
$Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ is a
$(U(\mathfrak g),W(\lambda))$-bimodule with right action
$u\cdot\bar v=\overline{v\,\eta(u)}$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]).

The **Whittaker category** $\mathcal C(\lambda)$ is the category of
$\mathfrak g$-modules on which $x-\chi(x)$ acts locally nilpotently for every
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). For
$M\in\mathcal C(\lambda)$ the **Whittaker vectors**
$$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=\{v\in M:xv=\chi(x)v\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}$$
form a $W(\lambda)$-module with $u\cdot v=\eta(u)v$, and
$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$.

The verification below establishes the algebra and module structures just
stated. The associated graded of the loop filtration on $U(\mathfrak p)$ makes
$W(\lambda)$ a filtered deformation of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$; that statement is
proved later on this page
([[thm-the-loop-filtration-on-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-has-associated-graded-u-of-g-e]]),
and the filtration used is the loop (good) filtration, not the Kazhdan
filtration.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a Lie algebra over $k$. In $T(\mathfrak g)$, regard
$[x,y]\in\mathfrak g$ as an element of tensor degree one, and let $I$ be the
two-sided ideal generated by

$$x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\qquad(x,y\in\mathfrak g).$$

The **universal enveloping algebra** is

$$U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/I.$$

Write

$$\iota_{\mathfrak g}:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow U(\mathfrak g)$$

for the composite of the degree-one inclusion with the quotient map. This
definition makes $U(\mathfrak g)$ a unital associative algebra and $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ a
linear map. It does not assert that $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ is injective; that conclusion will
come from PBW.

For a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ over $k$ and a $\mathfrak g$-module $M$,
the degree-$n$ **Chevalley–Eilenberg cochains** are

$$C^n(\mathfrak g,M)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\Lambda^n\mathfrak g,M)\quad(n\geq0).$$

Set $C^n(\mathfrak g,M)=0$ for $n<0$. Since
$\Lambda^0\mathfrak g=k$, evaluation at $1$ identifies
$C^0(\mathfrak g,M)$ with $M$. Cochains may equivalently be viewed as
alternating $n$-linear maps $\mathfrak g^n\to M$. No finite-dimensionality
or characteristic hypothesis is needed. If $n>\dim\mathfrak g$ in the
finite-dimensional case, the exterior power and hence the cochain space are
zero.

For finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$ and a short exact sequence
$0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$ of $\mathfrak g$-modules, the induced CE
complexes form a degreewise short exact sequence and yield the natural long
exact sequence

$$\cdots\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M')\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M)\to H^n(\mathfrak g,M'')\to H^{n+1}(\mathfrak g,M')\to\cdots.$$

Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition
of $N$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l\ge0$, so that $l=p_n$ is the number
of columns, and let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with matrix units
$e_{i,j}$ in the standard basis
$v_1,\dots,v_N$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]). Number the
boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left,
and for a box $i$ write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for its row and
column, $L(i)$ for the box immediately to its left (or $\emptyset$ if absent),
and $R(i)$ for the box immediately to its right (or $\emptyset$ if absent).
Define the nilpotent endomorphism
$$e=\sum_{i:\ L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g,\qquad ev_i=v_{L(i)},$$
and declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ for all $i,j$, so
that $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$ with
$\mathfrak g_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_{i,j}:\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)=r\}$.
Put
$$\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r,\qquad \mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0,\qquad \mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r,$$
and for rows $1\le i,j\le n$ define the shift $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ if $i\le j$
and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$
Finally let $\chi\colon\mathfrak m\to\mathbb C$ be $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$,
where the trace is the trace of the $N\times N$ matrix.

The verification below records the properties of this data that are used
throughout this page. $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$; $\mathfrak p$
is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor
$\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and
nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, while $\mathfrak m$ is the
nilradical of the opposite parabolic; the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ with
$s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ form a basis of the centralizer
$\mathfrak g^e=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,e]=0\}$; the box set
$J=\{(a,b)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$
is in bijection with $K=\{(i,j,r):1\le i,j\le n,\ s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}$ via
$(a,b)\mapsto(\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a))$, and
$$\xi_{a,b}:=\sum_{t=0}^{\mathrm{col}(a)-1}e_{L^t(a),L^t(b)}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)};$$
and $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character, $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$. This
grading is the type-A pyramid good grading of the source, not the Dynkin
grading attached to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple.

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

derivations.claim: Unit and counit. The adjunction between $Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}-$ and $\mathrm{Wh}$ has the unit $u_M\colon M\to\mathrm{Wh}(Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}M)$ and counit $c_M\colon Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}\mathrm{Wh}(M)\to M$ of [F2]. For every $M$, the kernel and cokernel of $u_M$ and $c_M$ lie in the kernel of the invariants functor: applying $H^0$ to the unit and using the vanishing of [F1] identifies the composite with the identity; a short exact sequence argument with the long exact sequence of [F3] then shows that if $H^0$ of a map in the category is an isomorphism then the map is an isomorphism, since the kernel and cokernel have vanishing invariants and a nonzero object of the category has nonzero invariants by [F1]. Hence $u_M,c_M$ are isomorphisms and the two functors are quasi-inverse.

Exactness and detection. Exactness of $\mathrm{Wh}$ follows because it is inverse to the exact functor $Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}-$ (tensoring with the right flat module $Q_\chi$, whose flatness is part of the free right-module structure of the source), and the detection statement is the case $H^0=0$ of [F1].

The transported tensor functor. For $M\in W(\lambda)$-mod and finite-dimensional $X$, the functor $M\mapsto\mathrm{Wh}((Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}M)\otimes X)$ is exact in $M$ because the composed functors are exact; it is the transport of $?\otimes X$ across the equivalence.

**Triangularity of the displayed tensor map.** Keep the polynomial-coordinate/distribution pairing from the good-grading calculation: the right-free PBW coordinates identify $Q_\chi\otimes_W M$ with the locally nilpotent coinduced model, by finite weighted Taylor pairing and descending leading-term subtraction, followed by filtered unions. Cofree evaluation on Whittaker vectors of this model tensored with $X$ gives a vector-space isomorphism $\ell:M\otimes X\to\mathrm{Wh}((Q_\chi\otimes_W M)\otimes X)$. It is not the inverse of the displayed $\mu_{M,X}$ in general. Choose a common Engel flag $0=X_0\subset X_1\subset\cdots\subset X_t=X$ for the nilpotent $\mathfrak m$ action, so $\mathfrak m X_j\subset X_{j-1}$; a negative-graded Lie algebra acts nilpotently on a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module. The matrix-coefficient construction of $\ell$ preserves this flag and has diagonal $1_\chi\otimes m\otimes x_j$: on each flag quotient the $\mathfrak m$ action is trivial, and the inverse cofree evaluation is precisely the unit $m\mapsto1_\chi\otimes m$. Every correction term involves a strictly flag-lowering matrix coefficient. PBW represents these finitely supported lifts by elements of $U(\mathfrak p)$ acting on $M$; no completion of $M$ is used. The displayed map applies $\eta^{-1}$ of this representative to $M$ and leaves the $X$ component in its flag position. Thus $A=\mu_{M,X}\ell$ preserves $M\otimes X_j$ and is the identity on its successive quotients. Write $A=1+N$; then $N^t=0$, although its off-diagonal entries can be arbitrary operators on $M$. Hence $A^{-1}=\sum_{r=0}^{t-1}(-N)^r$, and $\mu_{M,X}$ is a vector-space isomorphism. This argument distinguishes cofree constant evaluation from the extension-dependent displayed map.

Associativity. The associativity isomorphisms of the transported functor are obtained by inserting the canonical associativity isomorphisms of the tensor product of $\mathfrak g$-modules into the definition of $\circledast$ and applying the inverse equivalence; they are compatible by the naturality of the unit and counit of the adjunction and by the coherence of the tensor associativity in $\mathcal C(\lambda)$.

**Balancing and $W$-linearity.** PBW gives unique representatives $\eta(u)1_\chi$, $u\in U(\mathfrak p)$, in $Q_\chi$. Define $\psi_M(\eta(u)1_\chi\otimes m)=um$. Since the right action of $w\in W\subset U(\mathfrak p)$ sends this representative to $\eta(uw)1_\chi$, the formula is right-$W$-balanced: $(uw)m=u(wm)$. Moreover $\psi_M(\eta(v)q\otimes m)=v\psi_M(q\otimes m)$ for $v\in U(\mathfrak p)$. The shift $\eta$ adds a Lie character on $\mathfrak p$, so on its primitive generators, and hence multiplicatively on $U(\mathfrak p)$, $(\eta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(v)=\Delta\eta(v)$. The $W$ action on the source Whittaker subspace is therefore $\Delta\eta(w)$, while the target restricted $\mathfrak p$-module $M\otimes X$ has action $\Delta(w)$. No equality with cofree evaluation or citation-only character-equation argument is used.

Independence of the order.
